clue.text: I gag on a cored root vegetable

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another follows it, so the I-and-gag part comes after
a cored fruit has its middle removed, so only the outside letters of the word root are kept

parts.note: to gag is to choke

explanation.surface: Someone retches over a hollowed-out root vegetable they are trying to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Root vegetable' looks like one phrase, but 'root' is wordplay and 'vegetable' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The globe artichoke is a thistle-like plant whose flower head is eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Royal secret police allowed into three articles

indicators.note: being allowed into a place means going inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: AN, A and A are three indefinite articles, written one after another
the Stasi was the East German secret police

explanation.surface: East German agents are let in among a few grammar words, as if spying on a royal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stasi goes between the second and third articles: AN + A + STASI + A.
explanation.definitionFit: Anastasia was the youngest daughter of the last Russian tsar, a grand duchess and so a royal.

clue.text: On the contrary, I love marijuana themes in literature!

indicators.note: taking things the contrary way round here means the pieces are read backwards, upwards in this down entry

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
pot is slang for marijuana

explanation.surface: A student cheekily declares their love of cannabis is the true literary theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' sounds like a debating contradiction but it turns I O POT round.
explanation.definitionFit: Topoi, the plural of topos, are conventional motifs or commonplaces used repeatedly in literature.

clue.text: Not having a tot or two riled chef up

definitions.text: Not having a tot or two

indicators.note: stirred up, so the letters of riled chef are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A chef gets annoyed, and the line suggests children are the cause or the cure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' here is a small child, not a measure of drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with no children by choice is described this way, a tot or two being a child or children.

clue.text: Lake beside a port, time to get in!

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one letter goes inside the run of the others

parts.note: on can mean beside, as in a house on the river
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port, often just Rio

explanation.surface: A traveller at a lakeside port is told it is time to board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get in' places the time letter after the first two letters, splitting the run.
explanation.definitionFit: Ontario is one of the five Great Lakes of North America, on the Canada–US border.

clue.text: English soldier seen around section is simply ingenious

indicators.note: a piece seen around another wraps round it, so the two outer pieces enclose the middle one

parts.note: a soldier ant is a worker caste, so soldier gives ant
a leg is a section of a journey or race

explanation.surface: A British soldier spotted near a part of something judges it a clever piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen around' means the English and soldier pieces enclose the section; 'simply ingenious' describes a neat solution, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegant solution or proof is one that is clever while being pleasingly simple.

clue.text: Criminals purchasing island? They're minted!

indicators.note: purchasing something means taking it in, so the word for criminals holds the island letter

parts.note: cons are convicts, so criminals

explanation.surface: Crooks buying an island must be rolling in money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minted' is British slang for very rich, which fits the crooks, but the definition reads it literally: coins are struck at a mint.
explanation.definitionFit: Coins are produced by a mint, so they are literally the things that get minted.

clue.text: Cocaine high and drops of potent Armenian brew

parts.note: C is slang shorthand for cocaine
up means high, as in a plane being up

indicators.note: only a drop of each word is taken, here its first letter

explanation.surface: A drug high is mixed with a strong Armenian concoction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brew' suggests something potent, but a cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A brew is British slang for a pot or cup of tea, which is also what a cuppa means.

clue.text: Old person realities sent off the rails

indicators.note: something off the rails has gone wild, so the letters of realities are disordered

explanation.surface: An elderly person loses their grip on what is real.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old person' looks like a pensioner, but it means a person of ancient times.
explanation.definitionFit: An Israelite was a member of the ancient Hebrew people of the Old Testament, so a person of old.

clue.text: Sting and Summers essentially invested in small paintings

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: art can mean paintings collectively

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its centre, so the middle letter of Summers is taken

explanation.surface: Sting and Andy Summers, bandmates in the Police, turn up in some little pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: Sting and Andy Summers were members of the rock band the Police, but here 'Sting' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To smart is to feel a sharp stinging pain, so sting and smart are synonyms.

clue.text: I got the job! So at last tucked into a quiet beer and some drugs

parts.note: P is piano, quiet in music

indicators.note: something tucked into another is put inside it

parts.note: a pint is a glass of beer

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of So

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so two of them, Es, are some drugs

explanation.surface: A new hire celebrates with a quiet beer and something stronger.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an exclamation the answer might make.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has just been given a post could say these words, being the person appointed.

clue.text: Coat boat in paint artfully at the bow

indicators.note: one piece is placed in another
the bow is the front of a ship, so the front letters of paint and artfully are taken

parts.note: an ark is a boat, like Noah's

explanation.surface: Someone coats a boat with paint, taking care at the front end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat' looks like a verb about painting, but it is the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A parka is a hooded windproof jacket, so a kind of coat.

clue.text: Tense editor, after taking religious instruction, had a shot

indicators.note: the editor comes after the religious instruction it has taken on

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
RI is the abbreviation for religious instruction, a British school subject

explanation.surface: A nervous editor takes a scripture class and then has a go at something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective describing the editor.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a shot at something is to attempt it, so it means tried.

clue.text: Stick around area to meet a bloke and a US highwayman

indicators.note: the stick goes around the area letter, holding it

parts.note: a rod is a stick
gent is short for gentleman, a bloke

explanation.surface: A man with a walking stick meets a fellow, who turns out to be an American robber.
explanation.walkthrough: ROD holds A to make ROAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A road agent was a nineteenth-century American term for a robber who held up stagecoaches.

clue.text: Senior and half-cut wino drinking beer and port

indicators.note: drinking takes something in, so the senior letters hold the beer

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: half of the word wino is cut away, so only its second half is kept

explanation.surface: An elderly man and a tipsy drunk are knocking back beer and port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, apt for a wino, but here it cuts the word in half. 'Port' looks like the drink; it is a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Salerno is a seaport in southern Italy, south of Naples.

clue.text: After eating delicious starter, munched meal with one's drinks

indicators.note: having eaten something means holding it inside, so the jumbled letters take in another
munched food is chewed up, so the letters of meal and one's are jumbled
a starter comes first, so the first letter of delicious is taken

explanation.surface: After a tasty first course, someone munches their meal along with drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: D, from 'delicious starter', goes into the anagram of MEAL and ONES.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemonades are sweet citrus-flavoured soft drinks.

clue.text: Flipping party time? Pops off to get drinks!

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the party and time letters are read backwards

parts.note: a do is a party
to pop off is slang for to die

explanation.surface: An exasperated host declares a party over and goes off for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive but it turns DO T round to TOD. 'Pops' looks like Dad.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is a hot drink of spirits, sugar and water, often taken for a cold.

clue.text: Give diet up, having eaten last of this?

definitions.text: Give diet up, having eaten last of this?

indicators.note: having eaten something means it is now inside, so the jumbled letters take in another
stirred up, so the letters of give diet are mixed into a new order
the last of a word is its final letter, here the end of this

explanation.surface: A dieter gives up the regime after finishing off the biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: S, the last of 'this', goes into the anagram of GIVE DIET. The whole clue also hints at a biscuit that ends a diet.
explanation.definitionFit: A digestive is a semi-sweet British biscuit, the kind that would tempt a dieter to give up.

clue.text: He's a spy in Barking that's both tough and useless

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters of he's a spy in are scrambled

explanation.surface: A spy is posted to Barking, a London suburb, on a hard and pointless mission.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is also a district of east London, which suits the spy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever, so a Sisyphean labour is endless, arduous and futile.

clue.text: With no goals, direct girl to sub American for European

parts.note: to aim is to direct something at a target

indicators.note: to sub is to substitute, so one letter of the girl's word is swapped for another

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A coach sends on a girl as an American substitute for a European player.
explanation.walkthrough: The A of LASS is replaced by E to give LESS; the clue's 'sub American for European' is read as swapping the American letter out.
explanation.definitionFit: Aimless means lacking purpose or direction, so having no goals.

clue.text: Ring work after bit of spoilt seafood

indicators.note: the ring and work pieces come after the letter from spoilt
only a bit of the word is used, here its first letter

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A phone call after a bad piece of shellfish, to complain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a circle or jewellery; it is a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: A scallop is a shellfish with a fan-shaped shell, eaten as seafood.

clue.text: Go back out with foremost of Romeos for a start!

indicators.note: the letter goes at the start of the other piece
foremost means first, so the first letter of Romeos is taken

parts.note: egress is a way out

explanation.surface: A man tells the leading Romeo to retreat and get out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like part of the definition, but it is EGRESS, an exit.
explanation.definitionFit: To regress is to return to an earlier or worse state, so to go back.

clue.text: One soon to make a bloomer got up and sat on friend

definitions.text: One soon to make a bloomer

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: rose is the past of rise, so got up
bud is American slang for a friend

explanation.surface: Someone about to blunder stands up and then sits on a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a gaffe, but here it is something that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosebud is an unopened rose flower, which will soon bloom.

clue.text: Broken many bones? Certainly not!

indicators.note: broken things are smashed apart, so the letters of many bones are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worried friend asks after an accident whether lots of bones were fractured, and is reassured.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of MANY BONES gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic denial, equivalent to not at all.

clue.text: Bed woman, having had bottom pinched

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom is the last letter, and pinched means stolen, so it is removed

parts.note: Bertha is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman takes to bed after someone has pinched her bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' suggests a nip but means stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: A berth is a bunk or sleeping place on a ship or train, so a bed.

clue.text: Butch Cassidy finally goes after chap heading for Louisiana

indicators.note: the last piece follows the others

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here of Louisiana
finally points to the last letter of Cassidy

explanation.surface: The outlaw Butch Cassidy heads off after a man bound for Louisiana.
explanation.walkthrough: Butch Cassidy was a famous American outlaw, but here 'Butch' is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Butch means aggressively masculine in manner, close in sense to manly.

clue.text: Son with affected mannerisms is a little rascal

parts.note: camp means exaggeratedly theatrical or affected

explanation.surface: A parent describes a showy, theatrical son as a cheeky child.
explanation.walkthrough: S and CAMP are side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A scamp is a mischievous child, a young rogue.

clue.text: Male idiot behind opening of Avengers Assemble

indicators.note: the male and idiot pieces come behind the first letter
the opening of a word is its first letter, here of Avengers

parts.note: an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A man in the film audience sits behind at the start of Avengers Assemble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avengers Assemble' is the British title of the 2012 Marvel film, but 'Assemble' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble things is to gather or collect them together, a sense of amass.

clue.text: Managed to collar canine that's released bit of ghastly gas

indicators.note: to collar is to grab round the neck, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: ran means managed, as in ran a business

indicators.note: released means let go, so a letter is dropped from the dog word

parts.note: a dog is a canine

indicators.note: only a bit of the word is taken, its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone manages to grab a dog that has let off a whiff of horrible gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's released bit of ghastly' means the canine word loses the first letter of ghastly; 'to collar' then wraps the managed word round what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Radon is a radioactive noble gas, chemical element number 86.

clue.text: A bit cruel to get plastered in oil?

indicators.note: plastered is slang for very drunk, so the letters of a bit cruel are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it rather unkind to be slathered in oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered in oil' paints a coating, but 'plastered' means drunk, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To oil a machine is to grease it so parts move smoothly, which is to lubricate it.

clue.text: Like the sound of Serpent in a childish tantrum?

definitions.meaning: a snake's noise is a sibilant sss, so this means sibilant like a snake
a petulant outburst, so in such a tantrum

explanation.surface: A snake throws a petulant fit.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense comes from the informal phrase 'hissy fit'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a snake-like sibilant sound and, from 'hissy fit', a sulky temper.

clue.text: Odd sort of awful penis droop? Not I!

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are jumbled
not means without, so the I is taken out of the jumbled letters

explanation.surface: A man denies suffering an embarrassing drooping problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of PENIS DROOP, minus I, are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A pod person is a conformist or emotionless oddball, from Invasion of the Body Snatchers.
